title: Abdominal Examination
subject: Medicine
summary: A systematic bedside abdominal exam reveals organ size, tenderness, fluid and vascular signs. In low‑resource settings focus on findings that guide urgent management when imaging is limited.

sections.p: The abdominal examination is a structured physical assessment to detect disease of the gastrointestinal tract, solid organs, vasculature and peritoneum.
b: Inspection, auscultation, percussion, palpation (IPPP) is the classic order.
Goal: locate pain, identify masses, assess bowel activity, detect fluid or organ enlargement.

sections.p: Severity is judged by the extent of tenderness, guarding, peritonism and systemic response.
b: Mild: localized tenderness without guarding.
Moderate: diffuse tenderness, voluntary guarding.
Severe: rigid abdomen, involuntary guarding, rebound – suggests peritonitis.

sections.p: Common causes in East African and other low‑resource hospitals are grouped by organ system and prevalence.
b: Infections: typhoid, amoebic liver abscess, tuberculosis peritonitis, schistosomiasis, HIV‑related opportunistic infections.
Obstructive: small‑bowel obstruction (adhesions, hernias, volvulus), large‑bowel obstruction (cancer, sigmoid volvulus).
Inflammatory: acute appendicitis, cholecystitis, pancreatitis, ulcer disease.
Vascular: ruptured ectopic pregnancy, splenic rupture, aortic aneurysm.
Systemic: sickle‑cell vaso‑occlusive crisis, severe malaria with hepatic congestion.

sections.p: Patients may present with pain, distension, vomiting, altered bowel habit, fever or shock.
b: Pain localisation guides organ focus (e.g., RLQ → appendix).
Visible distension suggests obstruction or ascites.
Visible peristalsis may indicate paralytic ileus.

sections.p: When ultrasound or X‑ray is unavailable, rely on clinical signs (e.g., shifting dullness for ascites, visible peristalsis for obstruction).

t.b: Is there free fluid or organ enlargement? Positive fluid → ascites, hemoperitoneum; organ size guides further work‑up.
Is there air‑fluid level or obstruction? Multiple air‑fluid levels → mechanical obstruction; paucity of gas → ileus or perforation.
Is there leukocytosis or anemia? Leukocytosis supports infection/inflammation; anemia may point to chronic bleed.
Is there dehydration or renal impairment? Guides fluid resuscitation and drug dosing.
Does immunosuppression explain atypical infections? Positive test prompts opportunistic infection work‑up.

sections.p: Identify features that demand urgent intervention.
b: Rigid abdomen, absent bowel sounds, hypotension → perforation or severe peritonitis.
Rapidly enlarging abdominal mass with pain → ruptured aneurysm or splenic rupture.
Persistent vomiting, inability to pass flatus → complete obstruction.

sections.p: Treat the underlying cause, support circulation, and monitor for deterioration.
b: Fluid resuscitation with crystalloids; avoid colloids if renal failure suspected.
Broad‑spectrum antibiotics (e.g., ceftriaxone + metronidazole) for suspected intra‑abdominal infection; avoid aminoglycosides in renal impairment.
Analgesia with paracetamol; reserve opioids for severe pain after ruling out ileus.
Surgical referral for perforation, uncontrolled hemorrhage, volvulus, or obstructing hernia.

sections.p: Re‑examine abdomen after 4–6 hours in acute settings; monitor vitals and urine output.
b: Educate on safe water, proper sanitation to prevent typhoid and amoebic disease.
Vaccinate against hepatitis B and encourage HIV testing.
Screen for schistosomiasis in endemic areas.
Right‑upper‑quadrant pain: gallbladder disease vs. hepatic abscess vs. right‑sided pneumonia.
Diffuse tenderness: peritonitis vs. severe malaria‑induced hepatic congestion.
Normal white count does not exclude early perforation; rely on clinical peritonism.
Ultrasound may miss small free fluid in early ascites; shifting dullness remains valuable.

whenToSeekHelp: Inability to pass urine or stool for >12 hours with severe pain

faq.a: Palpation can alter bowel sounds; listening first gives an unbiased assessment of activity.

faq.q: What does a positive shifting dullness indicate?
faq.a: Presence of free fluid (ascites) that moves with patient position.

faq.q: When is a rectal exam essential?
faq.a: If there is lower‑abdominal pain, suspected GI bleed, or to assess for masses/impaction.

exam: What is the next step after finding a rigid abdomen with absent bowel sounds? — Recognise peritonitis, start IV fluids, give broad‑spectrum antibiotics, and arrange urgent surgical review.
How does the pattern of bowel sounds help differentiate obstruction from ileus? — High‑pitched, frequent sounds suggest mechanical obstruction; absent or hypoactive sounds suggest paralytic ileus.

A patient with sickle‑cell disease presents with abdominal pain and a tender, enlarged spleen. What complications must you consider? — Splenic sequestration crisis and possible infarction; monitor for rapid drop in hemoglobin and shock.
Why is percussion performed before deep palpation in low‑resource settings? — To detect fluid or organ enlargement without causing pain that could mask findings.

Explain how shifting dullness is performed and interpreted. — Percuss from the flank to the mid‑line with the patient supine, then turn them onto the side; a change from tympanic to dull indicates fluid movement.
When would you avoid metronidazole in an abdominal infection? — In patients with severe hepatic impairment or known alcohol‑related neuropathy.

What clinical clues differentiate a ruptured ectopic pregnancy from a perforated ulcer? — Positive pregnancy test, amenorrhea, and unilateral pelvic tenderness point to ectopic; history of NSAID use and epigastric pain suggest ulcer.

How does HIV status alter your differential for abdominal pain in this setting? — Increases likelihood of opportunistic infections (TB peritonitis, CMV colitis) and atypical presentations of common diseases.
